paragraphs: This paper studies whether coordinating several language models can provide a practical alternative to relying on one increasingly capable model. It identifies weaknesses in how existing systems choose a model for a question, select a model to combine answers, and decide when combining answers is worthwhile.

The proposed framework, JiSi, makes these choices more adaptive. Its routing method considers information from both queries and responses to capture meaning and problem difficulty. It selects an aggregator using a support set that evaluates both answer-combining ability and domain competence. A further mechanism switches between routing and aggregation according to their respective advantages.

Across nine benchmarks, the authors report that orchestrating ten open-source models can surpass Gemini-3-Pro at 47% of its cost, while also outperforming mainstream baselines. These findings support collaboration as a promising way to improve capability and cost together in the evaluated setting. The broader connection to artificial general intelligence is presented as a possible research direction.
icml-2026-beyond-gemini-3-pro-revisiting.tldr: JiSi adaptively routes questions and combines answers from ten open-source models, surpassing Gemini-3-Pro at 47% of its cost in the reported evaluation.

paragraphs: Self-rewarding reinforcement learning offers a way to train reasoning models on unlabeled examples, but it can be unstable. This paper traces that problem to rewards tied too closely to the model’s own confidence. When a model confidently makes a mistake and rewards that mistake highly, training can reinforce the same error.

The authors measure this feedback using three quantities: reward noise, coupling between the policy and its rewards, and the imbalance between excessive and insufficient rewards. Their analysis finds that strong coupling amplifies confidence-related errors and produces a growing tendency to over-reward, limiting both stability and achievable performance.

Their remedy, RLER, combines rewards from diverse models, adaptively interpolates those rewards, and uses disagreement to guide rollout selection. This aims to weaken the feedback between generating an answer and judging it. Experiments report a 6.2% improvement over the strongest intrinsic-reward baseline and performance within 3.6% of verifiable-reward learning, alongside stable scaling with unlabeled samples.
icml-2026-breaking-the-self-confirming-l.tldr: RLER combines diverse reward models to reduce self-reinforcing confidence bias and improve the stability and performance of self-rewarding reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning methods that improve problem solving can create trouble for role-playing agents. Optimizing an answer for its immediate usefulness may weaken the character’s distinctive voice or persona. This paper treats that loss of fidelity as a mismatch between the training objective and what successful role-playing requires.

Character-Centric Group Relative Policy Optimization, or CRPO, changes the objective through three mechanisms. It separates task logic from stylistic rewards to reduce conflicts between their training signals. It adjusts optimization constraints to account for character complexity. It also uses generic responses as negative baselines, discouraging the model from drifting toward an undifferentiated style shared across characters.

Together, these mechanisms make character distinctiveness an explicit part of reinforcement learning. The reported experiments find improvements over existing methods in consistency, emotion, and other evaluated aspects. The result supports training role-aware reasoning with objectives that directly account for persona, so that better task performance can coexist with more faithful characterization.
icml-2026-crpo-character-centric-group-r.tldr: CRPO adapts reinforcement learning for role-playing by separating logic and style rewards, adjusting constraints, and discouraging generic responses.

paragraphs: Counterfactual explanations describe changes that would lead a classifier to a different decision. Their usefulness can weaken in sparsely populated parts of the data, where classifiers vary more. DensityFlow addresses this reliability problem by guiding counterfactual generation through regions that the data support more strongly.

The method represents generation as a continuous trajectory governed by a neural ordinary differential equation. A differentiable density score steers that trajectory away from uncertain, low-density areas. The score is learned through noise contrastive estimation, using a discriminator to estimate density ratios. This provides a density-based alternative to defining stability through expensive intersections across ensembles.

When the target classifier is a black box, DensityFlow trains a lightweight local substitute along the counterfactual’s generation trajectory. That focused approximation supplies gradients while limiting queries to the target. Experiments report better counterfactual validity under model multiplicity and substantially lower query costs than ensemble-based baselines, supporting density guidance as an efficient route to more robust recourse.
icml-2026-density-guided-robust-counterf.tldr: DensityFlow generates more robust counterfactual explanations by steering changes through well-supported data regions and using local surrogates to reduce black-box queries.

paragraphs: Detailed image descriptions are useful when vision-language models support reasoning or auditing. This paper argues that standard alignment objectives can work against that goal: maximizing likelihood and applying KL regularization can favor familiar, high-probability descriptions while suppressing finer scene details. The authors call this tendency the Likelihood Trap.

Their framework, Geo-RL, rewards coverage in a semantic representation space. It treats sampled descriptions as defining a geometric shape and seeks to maximize that shape’s volume. Determinantal point processes encourage descriptions to represent distinct semantic directions, making diversity part of the training objective. The authors also derive a closed-form reward that measures a description’s marginal contribution by leaving it out.

That marginal reward supports stable policy optimization toward broader visual coverage. Empirically, the authors report substantially richer descriptions and better detail coverage without sacrificing visual grounding. The finding suggests that explicitly rewarding complementary semantic content can improve long-form captions while keeping their added detail connected to the image.
icml-2026-escaping-the-likelihood-trap-g.tldr: Geo-RL rewards geometric diversity among image descriptions to improve semantic richness and detail coverage while preserving visual grounding.

paragraphs: Federated graph learning trains across clients without exchanging their raw graphs. Clients can differ in both node attributes and connection patterns, making shared training difficult. This paper emphasizes structural differences that existing approaches often overlook, particularly connection biases associated with local features, collection practices, or user preferences.

Fed-Kalter introduces a graph convolution built around Kalman filtering with learned dynamics. It treats structural representations as hidden states and neighborhoods enriched with node features as noisy observations. Each layer filters feature-induced structural noise as information passes through the graph. Global aggregation shares only structural parameters, leaving room for each client to retain local personalization.

This separates the knowledge intended for transfer from aspects that should remain locally adapted. Across 16 graph classification datasets in four domains, Fed-Kalter consistently outperforms the evaluated state-of-the-art federated graph methods. Additional ablation and hyperparameter studies support its efficiency, robustness, and ability to mitigate structural heterogeneity, strengthening the case for explicitly modeling structure during federated aggregation.
icml-2026-federated-graph-learning-via-s.tldr: Fed-Kalter uses learned Kalman-style graph filtering and structural parameter sharing to improve federated learning across clients with different graph structures.

paragraphs: Estimating a person’s three-dimensional pose from one image becomes difficult when joints are hidden and depth is ambiguous. Glimpse addresses these problems by explicitly learning anatomical geometry at multiple scales. Its central idea is to combine evidence around individual joints with continuous information along the limbs connecting them.

The first component uses structured, deformable sampling to collect both kinds of features. Limb information is then passed to connected joints, helping bridge gaps created by occlusion. The second component promotes consistency across the full body: it lifts coherent two-dimensional features into a canonical three-dimensional reference space, where a shared anchor guides fusion according to distance.

The two components connect local visual evidence with a common geometric reference. Experiments on Human3.6M and MPI-INF-3DHP report state-of-the-art performance, including stronger robustness when occlusion is severe or body articulation is complex. These findings support using continuous limb geometry and global spatial correction together to improve pose estimates when individual joints provide incomplete evidence.
icml-2026-glimpse-geometry-learning-of-m.tldr: Glimpse combines joint and limb features with a shared three-dimensional reference to improve single-image pose estimation under occlusion and complex articulation.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning for language-model reasoning needs to decide which parts of an answer deserve credit. The paper argues that common algorithms, including GRPO and DAPO, use a coarse signal because tokens within a response receive the same reward. This makes the training feedback insensitive to differences between individual generation decisions.

The authors propose Dynamic Entropy Weighting, which redistributes rewards using normalized measures of policy entropy. Entropy captures uncertainty in the model’s choices. Group Token Policy Optimization, or GTPO, uses these weights to give tokens distinct rewards and construct token-specific advantages. Sequence-Level GRPO, or GRPO-S, applies an analogous weighting design at the sequence level.

Here, entropy directly shapes how rewards are assigned, extending its role beyond a regularization term. The authors report new state-of-the-art results on AIME and MATH 500, outperforming prior entropy-guided baselines. These results support their weighting mechanism as a way to improve reasoning training through more differentiated credit assignment at token and sequence scales.
icml-2026-gtpo-and-grpo-s-token-and-sequ.tldr: GTPO and GRPO-S use policy entropy to redistribute rewards across tokens or sequences, improving mathematical reasoning in the reported benchmarks.

paragraphs: Tool-using language-model agents can carry out workflows across multiple interactions, which also creates opportunities for misuse. This paper addresses an evaluation gap: single-prompt tests do not capture how an agent may gradually assist a harmful or illegal objective over an extended conversation.

The authors introduce STING, an automated red-teaming framework that organizes an illicit objective into stages within a benign persona and adapts follow-up prompts to the target agent. Judge agents track which stages are completed. The accompanying analysis treats the first jailbreak as an event occurring over time, enabling discovery curves, language-based hazard comparisons, and a metric called Restricted Mean Jailbreak Discovery.

On AgentHarm scenarios, STING produces substantially more illicit-task completion than single-turn prompting and adapted conversational multi-turn baselines. Across six non-English settings, lower-resource languages do not consistently increase attack success or task completion. These findings show why agent evaluations need to examine sequential behavior and directly measure multilingual effects instead of assuming chatbot findings carry over.
icml-2026-helpful-to-a-fault-measuring-i.tldr: STING measures multi-turn misuse of tool-using agents and finds substantially greater illicit-task completion, with no consistent increase in success for lower-resource languages.

paragraphs: Distributed training depends on combining gradients across devices. Hardware can silently corrupt that aggregation without producing an obvious failure signal, slowing convergence or preventing it. This paper models the resulting errors as inconsistent gradients and theoretically analyzes how those inconsistencies accumulate into divergence between model copies.

That analysis motivates PAFT, a training system with dynamic, asynchronous parameter synchronization. PAFT-Sync periodically synchronizes parameters to counter divergence. PAFT-Dyn manages the cost through dynamic overlap with training and by scheduling synchronization frequency. The synchronization mechanism is also adapted to support SGD, momentum-based SGD, and Adam, making the design applicable to several standard optimization choices.

The authors implement PAFT within PyTorch Distributed and evaluate ResNet, GPT-2, and LLaMA-2 training on configurations spanning four to 32 GPUs. The reported experiments show effective protection against aggregation errors while preserving training performance. The contribution connects an analysis of error accumulation to a practical correction mechanism whose scheduling is designed to limit the overhead of fault tolerance.
icml-2026-identifying-and-mitigating-err.tldr: PAFT counters silent gradient-aggregation errors through parameter synchronization scheduled to limit divergence and training overhead.

paragraphs: Continuous vision-language navigation predicts successive waypoints while updating the agent’s estimated position. Errors in those updates accumulate, allowing the internal position estimate to drift away from the actual coordinates. That mismatch then affects later trajectory predictions, creating a persistent problem for navigation in complex environments.

NeuroKalman recasts this process as recursive Bayesian state estimation. It separates a prediction based on motion dynamics from a correction based on historical observations. The authors mathematically connect kernel density estimation of measurement likelihoods with attention-based retrieval. This connection allows retrieved historical anchors to correct the model’s latent state without gradient updates during that correction.

Memory therefore supplies evidence for revising the current estimate as navigation proceeds. On the TravelUAV benchmark, the method clearly outperforms strong baselines after fine-tuning with only 10% of the full training data, while controlling drift accumulation. The result supports combining learned trajectory prediction with explicit state correction, and distinguishes training the navigator from correcting its state during use.
icml-2026-mitigating-error-accumulation-.tldr: NeuroKalman uses retrieved historical observations to correct navigation-state drift, outperforming strong TravelUAV baselines with 10% of the training data.

paragraphs: Reducing a language model’s key-value cache requires deciding which stored token information remains useful. Existing eviction rules often use immediate scores as though those scores mean the same thing across attention heads. This paper argues that heads differ in their ability to predict future usefulness: some reflect immediate contributions, while others capture longer-term value.

LU-KV allocates cache budgets across heads through a global optimization objective. The objective values the additional long-term semantic information retained by keeping more tokens. To handle the resulting non-convex combinatorial problem, the method combines a convex-hull relaxation with a greedy solver based on marginal utility. Offline, data-driven profiling supports practical deployment.

This makes cache allocation sensitive to differences in predictive usefulness across heads. Evaluations on LongBench and RULER report an 80% reduction in cache size with minimal performance degradation, together with lower inference latency and GPU memory use. The results support optimizing retention for future utility, with the proposed solver providing near-optimal allocations.
icml-2026-predicting-future-utility-glob.tldr: LU-KV allocates cache space across attention heads by predicted long-term utility, reducing cache size by 80% with minimal reported performance degradation.

paragraphs: Different vision foundation models contain complementary knowledge, but combining them into one model can create interference between their representations. This paper addresses negative transfer during distillation, where learning from multiple teachers can make their strengths harder to preserve within a single undifferentiated model.

PRISM uses a dual-stream mixture-of-experts architecture to organize that knowledge into specialized modules. In its first stage, a router conditioned on the teacher directs experts toward distinct representational subspaces. This expertise deconstruction is intended to reduce conflicts during learning. In the second stage, the router learns to recombine those experts into computational pathways suited to downstream tasks.

The design makes specialization and task-dependent assembly central to integrating visual knowledge. Experiments on PASCAL-Context and NYUD-v2 report new state-of-the-art results. The authors interpret these findings as evidence that sparse, emergent specialization offers a scalable approach to combining diverse vision models, while addressing the feature conflicts that make monolithic distillation difficult.
icml-2026-prism-synergizing-vision-found.tldr: PRISM combines knowledge from multiple vision models by training specialized experts and dynamically assembling them for downstream tasks.

paragraphs: Ride-hailing platforms can hold requests briefly before matching passengers and vehicles in batches. Choosing the holding interval involves a trade-off between time spent waiting for a match and time spent waiting for pickup. Changing demand and congestion make this decision difficult, particularly when a model cannot represent shifts across places and times.

RAST-MoE frames delayed matching as a decision process that accounts for changing operational regimes. Its reinforcement-learning agent uses a self-attention mixture-of-experts encoder, allowing different experts to specialize automatically in different conditions. The architecture aims to capture richer spatial and temporal patterns while keeping computation for each sample modest.

On real-world San Francisco trajectory data, the 12-million-parameter model reduces average matching delay by 10% and pickup delay by 15%. The authors also report stable training without reward hacking, zero-shot generalization to two additional cities, and clear expert specialization. These findings support regime-sensitive representations for coordinating decisions under changing supply and demand.
icml-2026-rast-moe-rl-a-regime-aware-spa.tldr: RAST-MoE uses specialized experts to adapt ride-hailing matching decisions to changing conditions, reducing both matching and pickup delays in the reported evaluation.

paragraphs: Graph masked auto-encoders learn by reconstructing hidden information using graph context. This paper finds that similar reconstruction outcomes can conceal substantially different uses of neighboring information, with consequences for later tasks. It therefore focuses on the reconstruction process itself, including how consistently context is used and how broadly training covers the graph.

The proposed C2-GMAE makes three changes. Positional encoding provides an observable structural reference. Density-partitioned masking promotes coverage across graph regions. Amplifying heterophilic edges helps preserve discriminative relational information that might otherwise weaken during reconstruction. Together, these mechanisms address structural guidance, training coverage, and the retention of informative relationships.

Experiments across multiple benchmarks show improved downstream performance relative to graph masked auto-encoder baselines. The finding matters because successful reconstruction alone does not fully describe the quality of a learned representation. By explicitly shaping how neighborhood evidence contributes to reconstruction, C2-GMAE improves the usefulness of those representations for the evaluated downstream tasks.
icml-2026-reconstruction-outcomes-look-s.tldr: C2-GMAE improves graph representations by guiding neighborhood-context use, broadening masking coverage, and preserving informative heterophilic relationships.

paragraphs: Robotic reinforcement learning often relies on rewards computed from precise distances to a target. Such position information is frequently unavailable when a real robot must learn from visual observations. ReLAM addresses this obstacle by inferring spatial distances implicitly through keypoints extracted from images and learning rewards from video demonstrations without action annotations.

Its anticipation model acts as a planner, proposing intermediate keypoint-based subgoals along the optimal path to the final goal. These subgoals organize learning into a curriculum tied to the task’s geometry. They also provide a continuous reward signal for training a low-level policy conditioned on goals within a hierarchical reinforcement-learning framework.

The framework includes a provable sub-optimality bound. Experiments on complex manipulation tasks with long action horizons report faster learning and superior performance compared with state-of-the-art methods. The contribution connects visual demonstrations, anticipated intermediate progress, and dense rewards, giving the robot a structured learning signal when precise target-position measurements are unavailable.
icml-2026-relam-learning-anticipation-mo.tldr: ReLAM learns keypoint-based subgoals from action-free videos to generate dense rewards that accelerate long-horizon robotic manipulation learning.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning post-training can strengthen mathematical and programming reasoning while narrowing the model’s exploration. The authors observe that increasing sampling temperature no longer improves pass@n accuracy in the studied reasoning models. Their analysis finds sharply reduced uncertainty in final-layer output distributions, even though intermediate layers retain relatively high uncertainty.

Latent Exploration Decoding, or LED, uses that difference across depth. It cumulatively combines intermediate output distributions and chooses depth configurations with maximal entropy as candidates for exploration. The method changes decoding without adding training or parameters, drawing on uncertainty already present inside the model.

Across multiple models and reasoning benchmarks, LED consistently improves pass@1 and pass@16 by 0.61 and 1.03 percentage points, respectively. These measures capture success with one generated answer and with up to sixteen attempts. The reported gains suggest that intermediate layers retain useful alternatives after post-training, and that accessing those alternatives can improve both individual answers and performance across repeated attempts.
icml-2026-restoring-exploration-after-po.tldr: LED uses uncertainty retained in intermediate model layers to improve reasoning exploration and accuracy without additional training or parameters.

paragraphs: Multimodal language models lose visual-understanding performance when images are corrupted. This paper investigates whether explicitly recovering the damaged visual content can help. Its motivation is that feature alignment offers limited interpretability, while reasoning in text cannot itself restore missing pixel-level detail.

Robust-U1 develops visual self-recovery through three stages. Supervised fine-tuning first teaches initial reconstruction. Reinforcement learning then uses two rewards: SSIM for pixel-level structural quality and CLIP similarity for semantic agreement. Finally, the model reasons jointly over the corrupted image and its recovered version, incorporating both inputs into understanding.

Experiments report state-of-the-art robustness on the real-world corruption benchmark and superior performance under adversarial corruptions on general visual question-answering benchmarks. The authors’ analysis finds that higher-quality recovery directly improves reasoning performance. These findings support explicit visual reconstruction as a useful component of robust understanding, with training signals that attend to both image structure and semantic content before the model reasons over the result.
icml-2026-robust-u1-can-mllms-self-recov.tldr: Robust-U1 trains multimodal models to reconstruct corrupted images and reason over both original and recovered inputs, improving robustness in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Visual models trained on generic images can perform poorly in unfamiliar environments. Fine-tuning them requires scene-specific annotations and can cause forgetting. Sea² addresses adaptation through viewpoint control: it keeps perception models frozen and trains an agent to move toward views that make those models more effective.

The agent is a vision-language model trained as a low-level pose controller in two stages. It first learns from rule-based exploration trajectories through indoor scenes. Unsupervised reinforcement learning then refines its behavior using rewards derived from the perception model’s outputs and confidence. Training requires no downstream labels and uses scalar perceptual feedback to guide viewpoint selection.

On ReplicaCAD, the authors report improvements of 13.54% for visual grounding, 15.92% for segmentation, and 27.68% for three-dimensional box estimation. These results show that changing how a frozen perception model observes an environment can improve task performance. The approach makes active observation a means of adaptation while using off-the-shelf perception modules directly.
icml-2026-see-act-adapt-active-perceptio.tldr: Sea² trains a viewpoint-control agent using unlabeled perceptual feedback to improve frozen vision models across three indoor perception tasks.

paragraphs: Estimating gaze from appearance is difficult to generalize when labeled examples are scarce and datasets lack diversity. This paper develops a semi-supervised framework that combines a small labeled set with abundant unlabeled data. Its aim is to learn more transferable gaze representations while reducing the need for manual annotation.

Disentangled Subspace Contrastive Learning, or DSCL, uses Jacobian regularization to separate feature representations into subspaces associated with gaze components such as pitch and yaw. Within each subspace, the method exploits the ordering of gaze values for contrastive learning. This gives unlabeled data a role in learning structured representations of the different gaze components.

Experiments across multiple benchmarks report competitive performance using 20%, 10%, and even 5% of the annotated data, under both in-domain and cross-domain evaluation. The authors also describe the framework as plug-and-play. These findings support combining component-specific representations with ordinal contrastive learning to make better use of unlabeled examples and reduce annotation demands.
icml-2026-semi-supervised-gaze-estimatio.tldr: DSCL separates gaze features into component-specific subspaces and uses unlabeled data for contrastive learning, achieving competitive results with as little as 5% of annotations.

paragraphs: Natural-language queries over time-series databases may ask for events, intervals, shapes, or anomalies across very long records. These requests pose two problems: ordinary text-to-SQL methods do not directly handle continuous signal patterns, and time-series models struggle with histories at database scale. Sonar-TS combines database search with signal-level verification to address both.

Its first stage uses SQL over a feature index to identify candidate time windows. Its second stage generates Python programs that inspect the raw signals and verify whether those candidates satisfy the request. This separates finding promising intervals from checking the detailed temporal behavior that makes an interval relevant.

The authors also introduce NLQTSBench, presented as the first large-scale benchmark for natural-language querying over database-scale time-series histories. Experiments show Sonar-TS handling complex temporal queries where traditional methods fail. The contribution provides both a search-then-verify framework and an evaluation standard for a setting that combines natural-language intent, long histories, and continuous signal structure.
icml-2026-sonar-ts-search-then-verify-na.tldr: Sonar-TS answers natural-language time-series queries by retrieving candidate intervals with SQL and verifying their raw signals with generated Python programs.

paragraphs: Having several language-model agents debate an answer can improve reasoning, but the discussion can still end in decisions compromised by faulty reasoning. This paper calls that failure debate collapse and develops a way to diagnose it through behavioral uncertainty at several levels of the system.

The proposed hierarchical metric measures uncertainty within an individual agent’s reasoning, uncertainty arising between interacting agents, and uncertainty in the system’s final output. Empirical analysis across several benchmarks finds these measurements to be reliable indicators of system failures. They therefore provide a diagnostic signal connecting individual behavior, interactions, and collective outcomes.

The authors then use uncertainty to guide policy optimization in the evolving debate. Training penalizes self-contradiction, conflict among peers, and low-confidence outputs. Experiments report consistent improvements in decision accuracy alongside reduced system disagreement. The contribution joins failure detection with a mitigation strategy: the same kinds of behavioral signals that reveal unreliable debates also help shape more reliable collective decision-making.
icml-2026-the-value-of-variance-mitigati.tldr: Hierarchical uncertainty measurements diagnose failures in multi-agent debates and guide training that improves accuracy while reducing disagreement.

paragraphs: Long chains of reasoning improve language-model performance but increase inference computation. Compressing them aggressively can remove logical content and damage accuracy. Extra-CoT addresses this problem with a training pipeline designed to preserve the meaning of reasoning traces while substantially reducing their token budgets.

The pipeline first trains a dedicated compressor on mathematical reasoning data with fine-grained annotations. A language model then learns from the compressed examples at multiple compression ratios, giving it experience with different budgets and preparing it for reinforcement learning. Constrained and Hierarchical Ratio Policy Optimization supplies a hierarchical reward that explicitly encourages successful problem solving under smaller budgets.

Experiments on three mathematical reasoning benchmarks report advantages over existing approaches. On MATH-500 with Qwen3-1.7B, Extra-CoT reduces tokens by more than 73% while improving accuracy by a reported 0.6%. This example shows that substantial compression can coexist with preserved or improved answer quality in the evaluated setting when both supervision and reinforcement-learning rewards account for constrained reasoning.
icml-2026-towards-efficient-large-langua.tldr: Extra-CoT combines semantically preserved compression, mixed-budget fine-tuning, and hierarchical reinforcement learning to shorten mathematical reasoning while maintaining answer quality.

paragraphs: Retrievers, rerankers, and reward models serve different purposes, but each assigns scores to text. This paper uses that shared structure to unify adversarial robustness research across these roles. An attack has a directly testable outcome when irrelevant or rejected text receives a higher score than relevant or preferred text.

This common definition makes it possible to adapt attacks and adversarial training methods across applications. The authors find that current training formulations often generalize poorly beyond the attacks they address. They introduce multiple training methods and show that combining complementary approaches can provide strong robustness while also improving ordinary task effectiveness.

The paper also examines reward models used in reinforcement learning from human feedback. Its adversarially trained reward models reduce reward hacking and support training better-aligned language models. These findings connect robust text scoring to both retrieval quality and the reliability of learning signals, showing practical value in studying vulnerabilities across model roles through one evaluation lens.
icml-2026-unifying-adversarial-robustnes.tldr: A unified text-scoring perspective enables complementary adversarial training methods that improve robustness, task effectiveness, and resistance to reward hacking.

paragraphs: Detecting AI-generated video requires detailed perception as well as reasoning about what the content shows. The authors observe that multimodal language models can reason strongly while still missing granular visual information. VideoVeritas addresses this imbalance by combining fine-grained perception with reasoning grounded in observed facts.

The framework introduces Joint Preference Alignment and Perception Pretext Reinforcement Learning. During reinforcement learning, it uses general spatial and temporal grounding tasks together with self-supervised object counting. These auxiliary tasks strengthen perception and improve detection without making detection itself the direct reinforcement-learning objective.

For evaluation, the authors introduce MintVid, containing 3,000 videos from nine state-of-the-art generators and a real-world collected subset with factual content errors. Their experiments find that existing methods tend toward superficial reasoning or mechanical analysis, while VideoVeritas performs more evenly across diverse benchmarks. The findings support improving basic perceptual skills as a route to better video detection, with fact-based reasoning complementing the model’s closer examination of visual content.
icml-2026-videoveritas-ai-generated-vide.tldr: VideoVeritas improves AI-generated video detection by training fine-grained perception through grounding and counting tasks alongside fact-based reasoning.
